objective: Audit a payments Deployment and its Dockerfile for container-runtime risk (privileged mode, docker.sock mount, added capabilities, root user, writable root filesystem, no resource limits), apply a hardened configuration, enforce Pod Security Standards, and confirm with a clean scan.
successCriteria: You identified every risky runtime setting in the Deployment and Dockerfile and can explain why each is dangerous
You applied the hardened manifest, rebuilt the image from the hardened Dockerfile and enforced the restricted Pod Security Standard on the namespace
A re-run of the configuration scan reports no failures
hints: Start read-only: look at the live Deployment, the Dockerfile and what the runtime reports. Ask of each setting: what does a compromised app process gain from it?

Two settings hand the container control over the node itself: privileged mode and a hostPath mount of the container runtime socket. Root, extra capabilities, a writable root filesystem and missing limits widen the blast radius.

Adopt the prepared files (cp deploy/deployment.hardened.yaml deploy/deployment.yaml, same for the Dockerfile), kubectl apply, docker build, label the prod namespace pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted, then run trivy config deploy/ again.

range.scenario: You are the platform engineer for the payments team. A pre-production review flagged the `payments-api` Deployment in namespace `prod` and the Dockerfile it is built from, but nobody has written down what is actually wrong. Your job is to audit both with read-only commands and a baseline `trivy config` scan, work out why each risky setting matters in defender terms, then apply the hardened configuration the team prepared, enforce Pod Security Standards on the namespace, and re-scan until the findings are gone. Everything here is simulated: no real cluster is touched.

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: payments-api
  namespace: prod
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: payments-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: payments-api
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: registry.example.internal/payments-api:1.4.1
          ports:

          securityContext:

            runAsUser: 0
            capabilities:

            - name: app-data

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: payments-api
  namespace: prod
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: payments-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: payments-api
    spec:
      automountServiceAccountToken: false
      securityContext:
        runAsNonRoot: true
        runAsUser: 10001
        runAsGroup: 10001
        seccompProfile:
          type: RuntimeDefault
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: registry.example.internal/payments-api:1.4.2
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
          securityContext:
            privileged: false
            allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
            readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
            capabilities:
              drop: ["ALL"]
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: 250m
              memory: 256Mi
            limits:
              cpu: 500m
              memory: 512Mi
          volumeMounts:
            - name: tmp
              mountPath: /tmp
      volumes:
        - name: tmp
          emptyDir: {}
artifacts.note: Change proposed by the security team. Review every line before adopting it.

artifacts.name: deploy/Dockerfile.hardened
artifacts.content:
FROM python:3.12-slim
RUN groupadd --system --gid 10001 app && useradd --system --uid 10001 --gid app app
WORKDIR /app
COPY --chown=app:app . /app
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
USER 10001
HEALTHCHECK CMD python -c "import urllib.request; urllib.request.urlopen('http://127.0.0.1:8080/healthz')"
EXPOSE 8080
CMD ["python", "server.py"]
artifacts.note: Proposed Dockerfile: pinned base, non-root user, healthcheck.

tasks.prompt: Which TWO settings in deploy/deployment.yaml give a compromised container the most control over the underlying node?
options: securityContext.privileged: true
A hostPath volume that mounts /var/run/docker.sock into the container
replicas: 2
The image being pulled from an internal registry
tasks.explanation: A privileged container is given nearly all host devices and capabilities and most kernel confinement is lifted, so the container boundary is largely gone. A mounted container-runtime socket lets whatever runs in the pod create and control other containers on that node, which is effectively root on the host. Replica count and registry choice are not node-level exposure.

tasks.prompt: Inspect the live Deployment and the runtime. Which securityContext field is set to true and removes most of the isolation between the container and the node?
tasks.explanation: securityContext.privileged: true (HostConfig.Privileged in docker inspect) is the single most dangerous container setting. It is rarely needed by an application like a payments API; if a workload genuinely needs one kernel capability, grant that capability alone instead.

tasks.prompt: Which host path is mounted into the container and gives it a handle on the node's container runtime?
tasks.explanation: The Docker socket is the runtime's control API. Anything that can talk to it can start containers with arbitrary mounts and privileges, so mounting it is equivalent to handing out node root. Workloads that build images should use a rootless/daemonless builder or a dedicated build service instead.

tasks.prompt: The container runs as UID 0, adds SYS_ADMIN and NET_ADMIN, and has a writable root filesystem. What is the defender's concern?
options: Root only matters on the host; inside a container UID 0 is harmless
Added capabilities only change network throughput

If the application is ever compromised, root plus extra capabilities plus a writable filesystem enlarge the blast radius: the process can reconfigure kernel-facing settings, tamper with binaries and persist changes
A writable filesystem only costs extra disk space
tasks.explanation: Container UID 0 is the same UID as host root unless user namespaces are used, and SYS_ADMIN is a very broad capability. A read-only root filesystem, a non-root user and dropped capabilities each remove an option from an attacker who has already found an application bug, which is the point of defence in depth.

tasks.prompt: The scan reports KSV011 and KSV018 (no CPU or memory limits). Why is that a security finding and not only a cost issue?
options: Limits encrypt the container's memory
A runaway or abused pod can starve the node and its neighbours (noisy-neighbour denial of service), and quotas and admission policy depend on limits being set
Limits are what make a container run as non-root
It is not a security issue at all; limits only affect billing
tasks.explanation: Without limits one compromised or buggy workload can exhaust node CPU or memory, evicting or slowing other tenants. Setting requests and limits also lets ResourceQuota and LimitRange govern the namespace.

tasks.prompt: Select ALL statements that are true about seccomp, AppArmor and read-only root filesystems.
options: seccomp with the RuntimeDefault profile filters which system calls the container may make, shrinking kernel attack surface
AppArmor applies a mandatory-access-control profile that confines a container's file, network and capability access
readOnlyRootFilesystem stops the process modifying its own image contents; paths that must be writable go on emptyDir mounts
These controls are unnecessary once the container runs as a non-root user
Setting privileged: true is fine as long as a seccomp profile is configured
tasks.explanation: The three controls are complementary layers: syscall filtering, mandatory access control and an immutable filesystem. Non-root does not replace them, and privileged mode removes much of the confinement they provide, so a profile does not make a privileged pod safe.

tasks.prompt: Apply the hardened configuration (adopt both hardened files, apply the manifest, rebuild the image, enforce the restricted Pod Security Standard on prod) and re-run the scan. Paste the attestation flag from the clean scan.
tasks.explanation: The clean scan proves the files no longer carry the findings; the compliance gate additionally checks that the change reached the cluster, that the image was rebuilt from the hardened Dockerfile, and that the namespace now rejects pods that would regress. Verifying after the fix is what separates hardening from hoping.

tasks.prompt: Which Pod Security Standards level, applied to the namespace with the pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce label, requires non-root, dropped capabilities, no privilege escalation and a seccomp profile?
tasks.explanation: Privileged is unrestricted, baseline blocks the known-dangerous settings (privileged, hostPath, extra capabilities) but still allows root, and restricted follows current hardening best practice. Pod Security Admission enforces the level at admission time, so a future manifest that regresses is rejected instead of silently running.

takeaways: Privileged mode and a mounted runtime socket remove the container boundary; treat either as a finding that blocks release.
Run as non-root, drop ALL capabilities, disable privilege escalation, use RuntimeDefault seccomp and a read-only root filesystem, and set resource limits.
Fix the source (manifest and Dockerfile in git), then enforce with Pod Security Admission so regressions are rejected, and verify with a re-scan.

objective: Review the RBAC of a shop cluster with read-only kubectl queries, find the over-privileged service accounts and wildcard cluster-wide bindings, replace them with least-privilege namespaced access, and verify the result with kubectl auth can-i.
successCriteria: You identified the service accounts bound to cluster-admin and to cluster-wide secret access
You removed the excessive ClusterRoleBindings and gave the CI service account only what its pipeline needs, in one namespace
kubectl auth can-i confirms the excess is gone and the legitimate access still works
hints: List the ClusterRoleBindings with -o wide and ask of each subject: does a workload really need this role, and does it need it cluster-wide?
Use kubectl auth can-i --list --as=system:serviceaccount:<ns>:<sa> to see the effective permissions of a suspicious service account. A wildcard in Resources and Verbs means cluster-admin.
Delete the offending ClusterRoleBinding, create a Role in the shop namespace limited to deployments (get, list, watch, patch), bind it with a RoleBinding, then verify with can-i.

range.scenario: You have been asked to review RBAC on the `shop` cluster before a compliance audit. Three workloads talk to the Kubernetes API: the `ci-runner` service account (namespace `build`) deploys new versions of the shop, the `web` service account (namespace `shop`) reads its own configuration, and `prometheus` (namespace `monitoring`) scrapes metrics. Over the years bindings were added whenever something failed with `Forbidden`. Use read-only kubectl queries to find out what each identity can really do, decide which bindings are excessive, replace them with least privilege, and verify the result. The platform's audit controller records its verdict in a ConfigMap once the effective permissions are correct.

artifacts.content:
WORKLOAD ACCESS NEEDS (from the owning teams)

build/ci-runner
  Pipeline step: kubectl set image deployment/shop-web ... -n shop ; kubectl rollout status deployment/shop-web -n shop
  Needs: get, list, watch, patch on deployments (apps) in namespace shop ONLY.
  Does not need: any other namespace, secrets, RBAC objects, nodes.

shop/web
  Needs: read the ConfigMap shop-config in its own namespace.
  Does not need: secrets, other namespaces.

monitoring/prometheus
  Needs: read-only cluster-wide (pods, nodes, endpoints, services) for scraping. Bound to the built-in view role.
artifacts.note: What each identity legitimately needs. Compare this with what it can actually do.

artifacts.name: change-guardrails.txt
artifacts.content:
PLATFORM RBAC GUARDRAILS

1. Workload service accounts must not be bound to cluster-admin.
2. No '*' in verbs or resources of any Role or ClusterRole created for a workload.
3. Prefer RoleBinding (namespaced) over ClusterRoleBinding. A RoleBinding that references a ClusterRole grants its rules only inside the RoleBinding's namespace.
4. Before removing or changing a binding, attach the effective permissions (kubectl auth can-i --list --as=...) to the change record.
5. Verify least privilege after the change; do not assume.
artifacts.note: The team's written rules for RBAC changes.

tasks.prompt: List the ClusterRoleBindings and compare them with workload-access-needs.txt. Which bindings are excessive for the workloads they serve? Select all that apply.
options: ci-runner-admin: the CI service account is bound to cluster-admin
shop-web-secrets: the web service account can read secrets in every namespace
monitoring-view: Prometheus is bound to the built-in view role
system:basic-user: the default binding for authenticated users
tasks.explanation: cluster-admin for a pipeline that only patches one Deployment, and cluster-wide secret read for a web app that needs one ConfigMap, are both far beyond need. The view role is the built-in read-only role and excludes secrets, which matches what Prometheus needs, and system:basic-user is a Kubernetes default.

tasks.prompt: Run kubectl auth can-i --list for each service account. Which service account (name only) shows a wildcard on every resource and every verb?
tasks.explanation: A row of *.* with verb [*] is cluster-admin in effect. kubectl auth can-i --list --as=... is the quickest way to see effective permissions regardless of how many bindings and roles combine to produce them.

tasks.prompt: What does a RoleBinding that references a ClusterRole (for example view) grant, compared with a ClusterRoleBinding to the same ClusterRole?
options: The same cluster-wide access; the kind of binding makes no difference
Access only to the cluster-scoped objects such as nodes and namespaces
The ClusterRole's rules but only inside the RoleBinding's namespace
Nothing at all; a RoleBinding cannot reference a ClusterRole
tasks.explanation: A RoleBinding scopes whatever it references to its own namespace, which is why reusable ClusterRoles bound with RoleBindings are a common least-privilege pattern. A ClusterRoleBinding grants the rules in every namespace and for cluster-scoped resources.

tasks.prompt: During an RBAC review, which of these permissions deserve extra scrutiny because they let a subject expand its own or others' access? Select all that apply.
options: create or patch on clusterrolebindings and rolebindings
the bind and escalate verbs on roles and clusterroles
the impersonate verb on users, groups or serviceaccounts
get on a ConfigMap in the subject's own namespace
tasks.explanation: Each of the first three can raise privilege beyond what the subject was explicitly granted: Kubernetes normally prevents granting permissions you do not hold, but bind, escalate and impersonate (and the ability to edit bindings) are the controlled exceptions, so they should be rare and reviewed. Reading one ConfigMap in your own namespace is ordinary least-privilege access.

tasks.prompt: The web service account only needs to read the ConfigMap shop-config in namespace shop. What is the right fix for its binding shop-web-secrets?
options: Delete the web service account so it cannot be misused
Keep the binding but rename the ClusterRole to something less alarming
Remove the binding and, if the app still needs API access, grant a namespaced Role limited to get on that ConfigMap
Bind web to the cluster-admin ClusterRole so it never hits Forbidden again
tasks.explanation: Remove the cluster-wide secret access and give back only what the owning team documented, scoped to the namespace and, where possible, the resource name. Deleting the service account breaks the app without fixing the policy, and widening access to stop Forbidden errors is how the problem arose.

tasks.prompt: Apply the least-privilege fix: remove ci-runner-admin and shop-web-secrets, give ci-runner a namespaced Role (deployments only, no wildcards) bound in shop, then verify with kubectl auth can-i (ci-runner cannot delete clusterrolebindings, can still patch deployments in shop, and web cannot read secrets across namespaces). Read the platform's attestation and paste the flag.
tasks.explanation: The audit controller only passes once all three verifications hold: the excess is denied and the legitimate access still works. Testing both directions matters, because a fix that removes access the pipeline needs just gets rolled back to cluster-admin at the next outage.

tasks.prompt: Which kubectl subcommand tests whether a user or service account is allowed to perform an action, including with --as impersonation?
tasks.explanation: kubectl auth can-i asks the API server's authorizer directly, so it reflects effective permissions after all roles and bindings are combined. Run it before and after a change, ideally in CI, to catch permission drift.

tasks.prompt: Besides tightening roles and bindings, which additional hardening steps reduce the exposure of workload service accounts? Select all that apply.
options: Set automountServiceAccountToken: false on pods that never call the Kubernetes API
Use a dedicated service account per workload instead of the namespace's default one
Review periodically with kubectl auth can-i --list and remove stale bindings
Put wildcards in the Role's verbs so rules are shorter and easier to audit
tasks.explanation: Not mounting a token where it is not needed, giving each workload its own identity and reviewing regularly all shrink what a compromised pod could do. Wildcards make rules shorter but silently grant verbs added in the future, and they are forbidden by the team guardrails.

takeaways: Review effective permissions (kubectl auth can-i --list --as=...), not just role names: that is where wildcards and stacked bindings show up.
Workloads get namespaced Roles with explicit verbs and resources; cluster-admin and cluster-wide secret access are exceptions that need a written reason.
Verify both directions after the fix: the excess must be denied and the legitimate access must still work.

objective: Replace broad node-role credentials with a correctly scoped IRSA trust policy for one Kubernetes service account, then audit and harden the worker node's instance metadata options (IMDSv2 required, hop limit 1) and verify the result.
successCriteria: You wrote an IRSA trust policy that only the billing/invoice-sa service account (with the sts.amazonaws.com audience) can use
You found the node's metadata options were weak and applied http-tokens required with a hop limit of 1
The compliance evaluation for the node reports COMPLIANT after your change
hints: Pods can inherit the worker node's instance role through the metadata service. IRSA gives each service account its own role instead. Ask what the node role can do and who can reach it.

A trust policy for web-identity federation names the cluster's OIDC provider as the Federated principal and must pin the sub (namespace and service account) and aud claims with StringEquals, not a wildcard.

For the node: describe-instances shows HttpTokens and HttpPutResponseHopLimit. Fix them with aws ec2 modify-instance-metadata-options --http-tokens required --http-put-response-hop-limit 1, then ask AWS Config to re-evaluate and read the result.

range.scenario: You run the platform for an EKS cluster `prod-eks` in account 111122223333. The billing service (service account `invoice-sa` in namespace `billing`) needs to read invoices from S3, and today it gets that access by inheriting the worker node's instance role, which carries a broad S3 policy and is reachable by every pod on the node. Your job: review how the node and the role are configured, write a least-privilege IRSA trust policy so only `invoice-sa` can use its own role, and harden the node's instance metadata options so pods can no longer reach the node's credentials. Use the terminal to audit and fix; the artifacts show the current configuration. Everything is simulated.

tasks.prompt: Compare giving the billing pods S3 access through the worker node's instance role with using IRSA. Which statement best explains why IRSA is the better design?
options: IRSA is faster because it avoids calling AWS STS
The node role is shared by every pod on the node, so any pod inherits its permissions; IRSA gives each service account its own role and short-lived credentials via a projected token
IRSA removes the need for IAM policies altogether
The node role cannot be restricted to S3, so IRSA is the only way to use S3
tasks.explanation: Node-role credentials belong to the instance, so every pod that can reach the metadata service shares them and the permissions must cover the union of all pods' needs. IRSA ties a role to one service account via the cluster's OIDC provider, so each workload gets only its own permissions and the node role can shrink to what the node itself needs.

tasks.prompt: Audit the node with describe-instances. What is the current value of HttpTokens in the instance's metadata options?
tasks.explanation: HttpTokens: optional means the older IMDSv1 style of simple requests is still accepted. Requiring IMDSv2 forces a session token obtained with a PUT request, which blocks the simple request patterns that commonly turn a server-side request forgery bug into credential exposure.

tasks.prompt: Why does setting HttpPutResponseHopLimit to 1 on the worker node protect the node role from pods that are not on the host network?
options: It limits how many credentials the metadata service will return
It encrypts the metadata response so pods cannot read it
The IMDSv2 token response has a network hop limit; a pod in its own network namespace adds a hop, so with a limit of 1 the response never reaches it
It makes the pod's request wait one second longer
tasks.explanation: The PUT response that carries the IMDSv2 token is sent with an IP TTL equal to the hop limit. Traffic from a pod crosses an extra network hop through the node's networking, so with limit 1 only processes on the host itself get a token. With IRSA the pods no longer need node credentials, so the hop limit can safely be 1.

tasks.prompt: Fix the trust policy of invoice-irsa-role (the policy you would pass to aws iam update-assume-role-policy). Only the service account billing/invoice-sa, presenting a token with the sts.amazonaws.com audience, may assume the role through the cluster's OIDC provider. Other service accounts, other namespaces, other audiences, other clusters and the node role must be denied.

tests.name: invoice-sa in namespace billing can assume the role
A different service account in the billing namespace is denied
A service account with the same name in another namespace is denied
A token for the wrong audience is denied
A token without a subject claim is denied
A different cluster's OIDC provider is denied
The worker node role cannot assume this role

tasks.explanation: The Federated principal pins the cluster's OIDC provider; the sub condition pins the exact namespace and service account; the aud condition ensures the token was minted for STS. A StringLike with wildcards on sub lets every service account in the cluster assume the role, and omitting aud accepts tokens issued for other audiences. Use StringEquals for both.

tasks.prompt: Which control actually stops pods from obtaining the node role's credentials from the instance metadata service? Select all that help.
options: Require IMDSv2 (HttpTokens required)
Set the metadata hop limit to 1 on the worker nodes
Move pod AWS access to IRSA so the node role can be minimised
Rename the node role so it is harder to guess
tasks.explanation: IMDSv2 and a hop limit of 1 limit who can obtain node credentials, and IRSA removes the reason pods ever needed them so the node role can be cut down to what the kubelet, CNI and image pulls require. Renaming a role is not a control: names are not secrets.

tasks.prompt: Audit the node's metadata options, apply http-tokens required with a hop limit of 1 (keep the endpoint enabled), ask AWS Config to re-evaluate the rule eks-node-imds-hardened, and read the compliance result. Paste the flag from the compliant evaluation.
tasks.explanation: Verification is part of the change: the instance reports the new options and the Config rule re-evaluates to COMPLIANT. Changing only one of the two settings leaves the node non-compliant, and disabling the endpoint outright can break components on the node that legitimately use metadata.

tasks.prompt: In the IRSA trust policy, which value must the :aud condition key match for tokens that are to be exchanged with AWS STS?
tasks.explanation: The EKS pod identity webhook configures the projected service account token with the audience sts.amazonaws.com. Checking it in the trust policy rejects tokens minted for any other audience, such as the Kubernetes API server's own.

tasks.prompt: You fixed the running instance with modify-instance-metadata-options. For a managed node group, what makes the fix durable?
options: Nothing more is needed: instance-level settings survive node replacement
Set MetadataOptions (HttpTokens required, HttpPutResponseHopLimit 1) in the node group's launch template so replacement and new nodes are created hardened
Disable auto scaling so nodes are never replaced
Attach an additional policy to the node role
tasks.explanation: Nodes are replaced during scale-out, rolling upgrades and AMI updates, and replacements are built from the launch template, not from the hand-edited instance. Update the template (see nodegroup-launch-template.json, which still shows optional and hop limit 2) and roll the node group, then keep the Config rule to detect drift.

takeaways: Give each workload its own role through IRSA; pin the OIDC provider, the exact sub (namespace and service account) and the aud with StringEquals.
Require IMDSv2 and use a hop limit of 1 on worker nodes, set in the launch template so replacements are hardened too.
Shrink the node role to what the node itself needs and verify with a re-evaluation rather than assuming the change worked.
